step.name: Step 1
step.text: Kitchen appliance hookup is one of those things that can cause major headaches if not coordinated properly. It's not just about plugging things in; it’s about making sure your kitchen is ready *before* the new appliances arrive. Here's a timeline of what usually happens and why it's so important.

step.name: Step 2
step.text: Phase 1: Early Layout & Utility Planning. This phase is crucial. You need to decide on your kitchen layout, including where each major appliance will go, along with the sink and main prep areas. This isn't just about aesthetics; it’s about ensuring there's enough space for door swings and clearances, and that utilities like electrical, plumbing, and ventilation can reach each spot. At this stage, you also need to confirm if any appliances require dedicated circuits or specific plumbing lines. This planning usually happens before any demolition or serious construction begins.

step.name: Step 3
step.text: Phase 2: Rough-in of Utilities. Once the layout is solid, the electrical and plumbing professionals come in to rough-in all the necessary lines. This means running new wiring, installing junction boxes, and laying out water and gas lines to their exact locations, all according to the appliance specifications. This must happen *before* any drywall is hung or cabinets are installed. Getting this wrong means tearing out newly installed finishes later, which nobody wants!

step.name: Step 4
step.text: Phase 3: Cabinetry & Finish Installation. With the utilities in place, your cabinets can be installed, and countertops, flooring, and paint can be finalized. It's important that the cabinetry provides the correct niche size for each appliance, so measurements taken in Phase 1 are critical.

step.name: Step 5
step.text: Phase 4: Appliance Delivery & Final Connections. This is the last step. Your appliances are delivered and hooked up to the pre-existing, correctly installed utilities. This phased approach, with clear coordination between the general contractor and sub-trades, helps avoid common issues like an appliance arriving and finding out there's no dedicated circuit ready for it.
